judgments.catchwords: Originating Summons for declaratory relief as to the true construction of the Last Will and Testament - testator’s intention as expressed in the words of the will read as a whole, and not his unexpressed subjective wishes - Second, the court will, so far as the language permits, prefer a construction that gives every clause some operative effect over one that renders any clause meaningless - where two constructions are reasonably open, and one produces an intestacy, be it whole or partial, while the other avoids it, the court prefers the construction that avoids intestacy - the court is not entitled to make a fresh will for the testator merely because it suspects that he did not mean what he plainly said - the court may inform itself of the testator’s actual circumstances at the time he made the will, this includes his family, his property, and his business relationships, to understand what he meant by the words he used, before concluding that those words are ambiguous or deciding how any ambiguity is to be resolved. - company is a legal person distinct from its members, and that a shareholder, even one holding practically the whole of the issued capital, has no legal or equitable proprietary interest in the company’s assets.

judgments.title: Tan Ai Hoon v Tan Hock Soon
judgments.catchwords: 1. This is a dispute between a sister and brother over a house in Ayer Itam, Penang. The dispute is in one sense straightforward. The Plaintiff seeks to bring to an end the present arrangement under which she and the Defendant hold registered interests in the Property. The Plaintiff invokes section 145 of the National Land Code. 2. The Defendant resists that course. The Defendant’s case is that neither the Plaintiff nor the Defendant is a proprietor of the Property within the meaning of the National Land Code. According to the Defendant, they are registered co-lessees and trustees of a private lease. Accordingly, he argues that there is no co-proprietorship to be terminated under section 145 of the National Land Code and that the Plaintiff has no locus to invoke that provision. The Defendant further submits that the requirements of Order 31 rule 1 of the Rules of Court 2012 have not been satisfied and that the Plaintiff cannot obtain an order for sale under that provision. 3. Their respective positions are therefore entirely at odds. 4. The determination of these issues may have consequences beyond the parties themselves, particularly in cases where persons hold registered interests in land as co-lessees or trustees under a private lease. However, that is not the question before this Court. The Court is concerned only with the rights and remedies of these parties. Those rights and remedies must be determined by reference to the National Land Code, the Rules of Court 2012 and the authorities presently binding upon this Court.
judgments.judge: YA Dr Choong Yeow Choy

judgments.title: LIM CHUAN HOCK & SONS SDN BHD v OJY SDN BHD

parties.label: PERAYU
names: LIM CHUAN HOCK & SONS SDN BHD

judgments.catchwords: 1 . A construction contract ordinarily begins with an award of the work and ends with the completion of the project. This case concerns what happens in between. The work has been awarded but the approval needed to commence the work has yet to be obtained. The contractor had been appointed and had carried out some preliminary works. The substantive works, however, could not proceed without the Commencement of Work. This led to the termination of the contract and a dispute over who was responsible for the failure to obtain the Commencement of Work and its consequences. 2. This is an appeal by the Appellant, Lim Chuan Hock & Sons Sdn Bhd ("the Appellant"), against the whole of the decision of the learned Sessions Court Judge at Georgetown dated 4 June 2025 in Civil Suit No. PA-B52NCVC-66-12/2022. 3. In the Sessions Court, the Appellant was the Plaintiff and the Respondent, OJY Sdn Bhd ("the Respondent"), was the Defendant. The Appellant's claim arose from a Letter of Award dated 19 October 2017, under which the Appellant was appointed as the earthworks contractor for the Respondent's development project. The Letter of Award incorporated the I.E.M. Conditions of Contract. 4. The dispute between the parties principally concerned the failure to obtain the Commencement of Work approval. The Appellant contended that the failure to obtain Commencement of Work was attributable to the Respondent and that the subsequent termination of the Letter of Award was wrongful. The Respondent contended that Commencement of Work was a pre-condition to the performance of the Letter of Award and that without Commencement of Work the contractual works could not lawfully proceed.
judgments.judge: YA Dr Choong Yeow Choy

judgments.title: ANIDA BINTI IDRUS v KHAIRUNNISA BINTI AHMAD DAMANHURI & ors
judgments.catchwords: There are cases in which the law is required to examine events that no judgment can undo. This is one such case. Nour Rania Asyifaa binti Yuseri (Asyifaa) was only one year and three months old when she died on 22.2.2022 while under the care of Taska My Mom Child Care Centre. Her death was, for her mother, a loss beyond ordinary measure. This Court acknowledges that human reality. Its duty, however, remains to determine the dispute with judicial detachment, upon the evidence adduced and the applicable principles of law.

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case
